claim_boundary: These stimuli test recognition and transfer of communication choices; they do not test trust, memory, persuasion, engagement or action.
randomization_rule: Randomize task order within phase while keeping each learner's baseline and matched post-task assignment recorded.

tasks.prompt: A project was expected to take two weeks but took six because a required dependency arrived late. Which response most clearly performs the communication job? A: ‘The team is unreliable.’ B: ‘We planned for two weeks; the dependency arrived in week four, so the schedule moved to six weeks. This does not by itself show why the dependency was late.’ C: ‘Everyone knows this always happens.’
tasks.boundary: Do not infer motive or personality from the comparison.

tasks.prompt: Describe one expected-versus-observed difference in an ordinary task using two sentences and one limit. Do not name a person as the cause unless you have separate evidence.
A speaker says ‘In short, bring your identification tomorrow’ after explaining a process. Is this primarily an explicit contrast? Explain why or why not.
tasks.boundary: A marker or change word alone is not proof of the underlying job.

tasks.prompt: Give a plain instruction without using a contrast marker, then explain how it differs from reporting an expected-versus-observed outcome.

A speaker says ‘Clear documentation reduces repeated questions. For example, our clinic added a one-page intake guide and saw fewer missing fields in one month.’ What must the speaker still avoid claiming? A: that the case illustrates the claim; B: that one case proves the guide caused the entire change or applies to every clinic; C: that the case has any relevance.
tasks.boundary: A case can illustrate without proving representativeness or causality.

tasks.prompt: State a general claim, give a labeled observed, reported, hypothetical or illustrative case, connect it to the claim, and state one limit. Use no identifying personal detail.
Someone names one dramatic incident and says it proves an entire group is dangerous. Is this a safe use of an example? Explain the missing boundary.
tasks.boundary: Vividness is not representativeness or proof.

tasks.prompt: Explain a definition directly without adding a case, then say when a concrete example would improve clarity and when it could distract or expose privacy.

Which response uses bounded personal detail responsibly? A: ‘I once missed a deadline on a group project, so everyone should work exactly as I do.’ B: ‘During one group project, I missed a deadline after misunderstanding the handoff. It taught me to confirm ownership; that experience does not establish the best process for every team.’ C: a detailed story naming a private colleague without consent.
tasks.boundary: Personal disclosure is optional and cannot become universal proof.

tasks.prompt: Make one communication point concrete with an anonymous, hypothetical or safely bounded event. State what the event illustrates and what it cannot establish.
You do not want to disclose a personal experience, but a listener needs a clear explanation. Is refusing personal disclosure a communication failure? Give a safer alternative.
tasks.boundary: No learner should be required to disclose trauma, identity or private information.

tasks.prompt: Explain the same communication point directly without a story, then compare the privacy and clarity tradeoffs.

Which sentence is most precisely qualified? A: ‘This will definitely solve the problem.’ B: ‘The early data suggest the change may reduce delays, but we need another month of records to test that interpretation.’ C: ‘Maybe perhaps possibly it could sort of help.’
tasks.boundary: The qualifier should match the claim and name a revision condition.

tasks.prompt: State one observed, predicted, interpreted or recommended claim. Add the smallest qualifier needed and name what evidence would change your mind.
A manager uses ‘we cannot know anything’ to avoid answering a question about a documented missed deadline. Is this good uncertainty handling? Explain the accountability problem.
tasks.boundary: Uncertainty must not erase known observations or responsibility.

tasks.prompt: State a fact that needs no hedge, then state a prediction that does. Explain why the qualification differs.

After explaining how a shared calendar prevents duplicate bookings, which closing is clearest? A: ‘Anyway.’ B: ‘The takeaway is to assign one owner to the calendar; this helps prevent duplicate bookings but does not replace schedule review.’ C: ‘You should agree with me.’
tasks.boundary: The takeaway must follow from the explanation and retain its limit.

tasks.prompt: Explain a small topic, mark one takeaway, name its support, preserve one qualification, and offer a next step.
A speaker ends a complex disagreement by saying ‘there is only one acceptable view’ without addressing the evidence. Is this a responsible summary? Explain what was compressed away.
tasks.boundary: A clear close must not erase essential uncertainty or valid alternatives.

tasks.prompt: Close a short explanation with an unmarked final sentence, then close it again with a marked takeaway. Compare clarity without claiming listener improvement.
